title: Develop Capabilities: Malware
summary: This sub-technique is the malware engineering side of capability development: writing payloads, droppers, loaders, backdoors, packers and command and control protocols, and sometimes preparing infected removable media. The emphasis falls on purpose-built code the adversary controls and can update, which is why one family may share configuration formats and protocol quirks across separate intrusions even when the compiled binaries differ. Some builders deliberately plant artefacts associated with a different known group, so attribution drawn from strings, certificate names or compile paths should be treated as a hypothesis rather than a conclusion. Defenders rarely observe the development itself; they observe the product, and the strongest leads stay behavioural.

beginner.definition: This is the part of capability development that covers malware. The parent technique includes all the tools an attacker builds, such as exploits and certificates. Here the tool is software that runs on a victim's computer. It might open a back door, steal files or hide other tools. The attacker builds it so that few people have seen the code before, which makes detection harder.
beginner.whyItMatters: Malware is the part of an attack that actually touches your systems. If it was written for one campaign, your antivirus may not know it yet. Builders can also hide clues that point to another group, which wastes investigation time. Custom malware can be updated after delivery, so it changes while you watch it. Traditional defences still help, but they are not enough on their own. Behaviour monitoring, good logging and fast response are what catch these tools.
howItWorks: The attacker decides what the malware must do, such as stay hidden or steal files.
Developers write the code and often split it into stages or modules.
They compress or obfuscate it so security tools cannot read it easily.
They test it against common defenders and change it until it passes.
They may leave fake clues that point to a completely different attacker group.
After the tool has been delivered, they update it again through its command channel.
beginner.example: Picture a workshop that makes one bespoke tool for one job. The tool is not sold in any shop and no catalogue lists it. A guard who only checks items against a list will let it pass. Later the workshop changes the handle so the same tool looks different again. That is how custom malware behaves. Each version may look new, but the job it does and the way it is used stay the same, which is what a careful observer can still notice.
takeaways: New malware has no known signature, so watch what it does.
Fake clues are common, so confirm attribution with several kinds of evidence.
Shared code or settings can link separate incidents to one builder.

objectives: Describe the kinds of malware that an adversary may develop in house.
Explain how this sub-technique differs from the parent capability development technique.
Identify behavioural evidence that reveals custom malware in action.
Explain why attribution based on embedded clues can be unreliable.
Relate malware development to the infrastructure the tool needs to communicate.
